findings.F1: The Calmar failed (0.291) because of two long falls: −69.5 % from w20 to w24 (491 days to the trough) and −58.4 % from w3 to w6 (439 days). Inside them the short side lost while the long side still earned: net summed gain −0.75 (342 bars) and −0.63 (259 bars) on shorts, against +0.27 (255 bars) and +0.12 (223 bars) on longs.
findings.F2: Over all bars the short side carries little and the long side carries the gain: mean gain per bar is +0.070 % on 1523 short bars against +0.311 % on 1361 long bars. Rebuilt with costs, the short-only book has Sharpe −0.13 and Calmar −0.15, while the long-only book has Sharpe 1.07, deepest fall −33.9 % and Calmar 1.04 (as tested: 0.63, −69.5 %, 0.30).

findings.F4: The gain grows with the size of the day's move, and small moves only pay fees:
findings.F5: The 5-day to 30-day volatility ratio grades the gain as the idea says: +0.001 % per bar in its lowest quintile and +0.578 % (t 3.05, n 436) in its highest. The rebound side is therefore graded by both of the idea's own measures.

ideas.idea: The larger XMR's one-day fall against its 30-day daily volatility, the more it rises back over the next day, and this rebound grows with how high its volatility over the past 5 days stands against its 30-day volatility.
ideas.consequence: A trader would buy XMR after sharp falls in turbulent stretches, sized by the fall and the turbulence, and would not short its sharp rises, which is the side that lost through the book's long falls.
ideas.name: rebound after turbulent falls

ideas.idea: The larger XMR's one-day fall measured in its 30-day daily volatility, the larger its rise over the next day, with the rebound growing faster than the fall, so that falls of more than a usual day carry most of it.
ideas.consequence: A trader would buy XMR mainly after falls well beyond a usual day and leave small down days alone, since those earn less than their trading cost.
ideas.name: rebound grows with fall
